title: The alchemist's elixir
hook: fix yourself first, or start helping as you are? two Buddhist answers, and an elixir
tomorrow: wanting to help, and helping. what's the gap?

segments.voice: Yesterday: lightning in the night. A good thought flashes and fades, and Shantideva asked what could hold the light. Here's his answer, in a metalworker's language.
screen: `LIGHTNING IN THE NIGHT.` → `WHAT HOLDS THE LIGHT?`

segments.voice: Every self-help shelf says the same thing a hundred ways: put your own oxygen mask on first. Get your life in order, then help others. It sounds wise, and it often is. Shantideva's poem says something that sounds like the opposite. Old alchemists dreamed of an elixir that turns base metal into gold. The wish to wake up for everyone, he says, is that elixir. It takes this ordinary body and turns it into something priceless. Not after you're fixed. Now.
screen: `OXYGEN MASK FIRST.` → `AN ELIXIR FOR BASE METAL.` → `NOT AFTER. NOW.`

segments.voice: Two real voices inside Buddhism, and each deserves its best case. First, Shantideva. The awakening mind, bodhicitta, is the wish to become awake for the sake of all beings. He calls it the finest alchemist's elixir: it takes this impure body and makes it into the priceless form of a Buddha. A verse earlier he goes further. The moment that wish arises, even someone stuck in the prison of suffering is called a child of the Buddhas. His point: you don't wait to be gold before you start. The elixir works on base metal. That's what it's for. Now the other voice, which many teachers lean on. The Dhammapada says, in its own way, set yourself first in what is right, and only then teach others. Elsewhere it warns against neglecting your own good for someone else's, however great. Its best case: a drowning person can't pull anyone out. Train the mind first, or your help gets tangled with your own anger and need. Here's where they meet. Shantideva's next chapters are mostly about guarding your own mind. And the Dhammapada's road is full of kindness. The argument is about the order, and both keep both. Base metal to gold.
screen: `THE ELIXIR: THE WISH TO WAKE FOR ALL.` · `IT WORKS ON BASE METAL.` · `THE OTHER VOICE: TRAIN YOURSELF FIRST.` · `BOTH KEEP BOTH; THEY ARGUE ORDER.` · then, large: `BASE METAL TO GOLD.`

segments.voice: Take a pen and write one small thing you'll do today that helps someone besides you. Then, under it, write one thing that keeps your own mind steady while you do it. Read both lines back once, and sit quietly with the page.
The alchemist's elixir: Shantideva's picture of the awakening mind. Poured on base metal, it makes gold, starting with whoever you are today.
Here's the line: base metal to gold, and nobody starts as gold. Four days into the poem; see you tomorrow.

howItsDone: In Mahayana communities, a practice session often opens by recalling the wish to awaken for the benefit of all beings; Theravada teachers often stress training one's own mind, with kindness for others built into that training.

fork.setup: your study group argues: help a struggling friend now, or sort out your own mess first? you're on Shantideva's side. what's the other side's best case?
options: a drowning person can't pull anyone out; help tangled with your own anger can hurt.
helping others is a distraction, so it's better to avoid it until you're done training.
other people's problems aren't your business, so there's no need to step in.
fork.reveal: that's the strongest form of the Dhammapada's view: train the mind so your help is clean. Shantideva's reply: the elixir works on base metal, so start as you are, and keep training.

original.note: Sanskrit: bodhi, awakening, and citta, mind: the mind set on awakening for the sake of all beings.

trapdoor: what you thought: you have to become a good person before you can do any real good.
what it means: Shantideva says the wish to wake up for everyone is an elixir that works on ordinary people, starting now.

what a scholar hears: an old question about order: the Dhammapada's 'set yourself right first' and Shantideva's 'the elixir works on base metal' are two emphases inside one tradition, not two sides that exclude each other.

chat.says: ava says i can't help ông on 4 hrs of sleep when i'm a mess myself. is she right?
options: Partly. Shantideva says start helping as you are, but guarding your own mind and sleep counts too.
Totally. Nobody can help anyone until their own life is completely in order first.
Not at all. Helping fixes you, so skip the sleep and give him every hour you have.
chat.meaning: Shantideva says the awakening mind works on base metal, so you start now; and both voices keep training your own mind alongside it.

bodhicitta.meaning: the awakening mind: the wish to wake up for all beings

Dhammapada.meaning: a collection of the Buddha's sayings in verse, in the Pali canon

alchemists.meaning: old metalworkers who sought to turn base metal into gold

Buddhas.meaning: fully awakened ones; Shantideva speaks of many

sources.ref: Bodhicaryavatara 1.9-1.10 (the moment it arises, one is called a child of the Buddhas; the awakening mind as the finest alchemical elixir)
Dhammapada 158 and 166 (set yourself first in what is right; do not neglect your own good for another's)

notes: Debate shape: Shantideva's 'start now' (1.9-1.10) and the Dhammapada's 'set yourself right first' (158, 166) are presented as two emphases inside Buddhism, with no school labels and no ranking. 'Rasajata' (the alchemical elixir) in 1.10 is rendered simply as the finest alchemist's elixir; confirm.
